drivingQuestion: How can the mishna imply a creditor may collect from a namesake when it earlier said no one else can present a note against them?
outcomeNote: The unit ends on the contradiction; the resolution lies in the next unit

segments.he: נִמְצָא לְאֶחָד בֵּין שְׁטָרוֹתָיו ״שְׁטָרוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן פָּרוּעַ״ – שְׁטָרוֹת שְׁנֵיהֶם פְּרוּעִין וְכוּ׳. טַעְמָא דְּנִמְצָא, הָא לֹא נִמְצָא – מָצֵי מַפֵּיק; וְהָאֲנַן ״וְלֹא אַחֵר יָכוֹל לְהוֹצִיא עֲלֵיהֶן שְׁטַר חוֹב״ תְּנַן!
segments.en: § The mishna teaches: If a document is «found among one’s documents» stating: The promissory «note against Yosef ben Shimon is repaid,» and both men named Yosef ben Shimon owed this man money, «the» promissory «notes of both of them are» considered «repaid,» as it cannot be determined which debt was repaid and which is outstanding. The Gemara comments: The implication of the mishna is that «the reason» this man cannot collect his debt is «that» this note «was found» among his papers; «but» if it was «not» suddenly found, rather he was always aware of its existence, «he could present» a promissory note against one of the men named Yosef ben Shimon and collect the debt from him. The Gemara asks: «But didn’t we learn» earlier in the mishna: «Nor can another present a promissory note against» either of «them?»

moves.summary: Lemma: a found receipt makes both notes repaid
Implication: had it not been found, he could collect from one of them
moves.about: the found-receipt clause implies a third party can collect from a namesake, while the earlier clause forbids it

moves.summary: But the mishna said no one else can present a note against them
